directions: Set out container-grown Majesty Palms in late spring once soil has warmed, choosing a site with rich, constantly moist soil since this Madagascar river-margin species is far thirstier than most landscape palms. Give it high shade or filtered sun in its early years and full sun once established, and mulch heavily to buffer root temperature swings at the northern edge of its range. Its dense, upright crown of soft feathery fronds reads as an instant tropical focal point beside pools, ponds, and courtyard entries. In zone 9, site it in a warm microclimate and be prepared to protect it during hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant this South American wax palm in full sun on well-drained soil in late spring, giving it wide open space to develop its stout gray trunk and stiff, waxy-blue crown.

directions: Plant this South American wax palm in full sun on well-drained soil in late spring, giving it wide open space to develop its stout gray trunk and stiff, waxy-blue palmate crown over many years. It tolerates seasonal flooding as well as periods of drought once its deep root system is established, making it useful in low-lying Gulf Coast landscapes. Space it well away from walkways since older leaf bases can be sharply toothed. Use it as a slow, long-lived specimen or avenue palm where a bold silvery silhouette is wanted.

planting.note: Install in full sun during warm months, giving it generous overhead and lateral clearance since it eventually forms one of the thickest trunks and largest crowns in the genus.

directions: Install this massive Caribbean sabal in full sun during warm months, giving it generous overhead and lateral clearance since it eventually forms one of the thickest trunks and largest crowns in the genus. It adapts to a wide range of soils, from sandy coastal ground to heavier inland loam, and tolerates both drought and brief flooding once rooted in. Reserve it for large-scale landscapes, parks, or long avenues where its massive fan-leafed canopy can be appreciated at full size. Young plants are slow to trunk, so plant it as an investment piece rather than for quick impact.

planting.note: Plant once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm, in soil that drains well but does not dry out completely between waterings; reserve for the most frost-protected zone 10-11 sites.

directions: Plant this Pacific-island fan palm in full sun to light shade once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm, in soil that drains well but does not dry out completely between waterings. Its nearly perfect circular fronds on a slender, ringed trunk make it one of the most refined specimen palms for courtyards and poolside plantings in the warmest zone 10-11 pockets. Feed lightly but regularly through the growing season since it is a moderately heavy feeder for a palm of its size. It has essentially no cold tolerance, so reserve it for the most frost-protected coastal or Florida sites.

planting.note: Establish from fresh seed or a nursery-grown offset in a well-drained bed with light shade to full sun; water regularly the first year to establish, then rely on natural rainfall except during extended drought.

directions: Establish this Australian cycad from fresh seed or a nursery-grown offset in a well-drained bed with light shade to full sun, since it tolerates surprisingly cool winters for a cycad once its root system is settled. Its dense rosette of long, arching, dark green pinnate leaves makes a strong architectural mass planting or understory accent beneath high-canopy trees. Water regularly the first year to establish, then let it rely on natural rainfall except during extended drought. It is exceptionally slow-growing, so plan for it as a long-term structural feature rather than a fast-filling accent.

planting.note: Plant in sharply drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; keep on the dry side, watering only during active summer flushes, since soggy soil in cool weather is its main vulnerability.

directions: Plant this southwestern Chinese cycad in sharply drained soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, taking advantage of its unusual ability among sagos to shrug off brief hard freezes into the teens once mature. Its stiff, gray-green pinnate crown on a low, often branching trunk gives a rugged, sculptural presence to rock gardens and dry Mediterranean-style beds. Keep it on the dry side, watering only during active summer flushes, since soggy soil in cool weather is its main vulnerability. It is an excellent substitute for King Sago in colder zone 8 gardens where Cycas revoluta struggles.
